This report provides a technical audit and legal analysis of Canada's Research and Development (R&D) tax incentive architecture, statutory frameworks, direct innovation grants, provincial and territorial regimes, compliance procedures, and judicial precedents as of November 2026.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Canada enacted the most consequential expansion of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program in over a decade. Under Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, and applies retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3.0 million to $6.0 million (increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund from $1.05 million to $2.10 million), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended access to the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time via a three-year average gross revenue test (which Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations [CCPCs] may also elect to use), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Administratively, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process that cuts expenditure-only review processing times in half—from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days—alongside AI-assisted risk assessment. Furthermore, on November 5, 2026, Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny) proposed a $930 million five-year "Past the Prototype" expansion to bring initial regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs into the SR&ED program for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day.

At the sub-national level, provincial responses to the federal reforms have created a sharply bifurcated compliance landscape across Canada's 13 jurisdictions. British Columbia (Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) made its 10% SR&ED credit permanent and aligned with the federal $6.0 million limit, $15 million–$75 million phase-out, ECPC eligibility, and capital expenditure restoration. Québec enacted a structural overhaul for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, repealing seven legacy R&D tax incentives and replacing them with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) at 30% on the first $1.0 million above an exclusion threshold and 20% on the excess, covering both R&D and pre-commercialization activities as well as capital property. Conversely, Ontario retained its existing $3.0 million expenditure limit on the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) while restoring capital expenditures acquired on or after December 16, 2024; Saskatchewan doubled its 10% refundable CCPC threshold from $1.0 million to $2.0 million without adopting the $6.0 million federal cap or ECPC rules; and Alberta maintained its independent $4.0 million cap on the two-tier (8% base / 20% incremental) Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) while excluding restored federal capital expenditures from the Alberta grant base.
1. Executive Legislative & Policy Overview (2024–2026 Reforms)
1.1 Macro-Economic Scale and Dual Administration of the SR&ED Program

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program is the cornerstone of Canadian federal innovation policy and the single largest source of federal support for business R&D in Canada. According to official Canada Revenue Agency program statistics, during the 2024–2025 fiscal year, the SR&ED program delivered $4.5 billion in Investment Tax Credits across more than 22,000 processed claims submitted by over 19,000 distinct claimants (supporting over 24,160 businesses annually across multi-year filing windows). For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, the CRA reported $4.9 billion in ITCs claimed and $4.6 billion allowed, reflecting a cumulative growth of approximately 50% in annual credit value delivered since fiscal year 2022. Across the most recent reporting cycle, approximately 96% of processed SR&ED claims resulted in allowed tax credits—with 90% of claims accepted as filed, 6% accepted with adjustments following technical and financial review, and 4% denied in full.

Unlike discretionary grant programs that operate through competitive call windows and fixed budgetary envelopes, the SR&ED program is a statutory entitlement embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and Income Tax Regulations. Any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada whose technical activities and related expenditures satisfy the statutory criteria of sections 37, 127, 127.1, and 248(1) of the ITA and Part XXIX (sections 2900 to 2903) of the Income Tax Regulations is legally entitled to claim the incentive. Administration is bifurcated between two federal institutions. First, the Department of Finance Canada formulates legislative tax policy, drafts statutory amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, and designates prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903. Second, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the program day-to-day through specialized SR&ED directorates, publishes administrative forms and interpretive policies, conducts technical reviews via Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and financial audits via Financial Reviewers (FRs), and processes both federal SR&ED claims and harmonized provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (for all offering jurisdictions except Québec and Alberta).
1.2 Chronological Trajectory of the 2024–2026 Legislative Overhaul

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, the federal SR&ED regime operated under tightened rules enacted by the 2012 Federal Budget: the basic ITC rate had been reduced from 20% to 15%, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) overhead rate had been stepped down from 65% to 55%, arm's-length contractor inclusions had been reduced from 100% to 80%, and all capital expenditures and equipment lease costs had been eliminated from SR&ED eligibility. Following national consultations launched by the Department of Finance in January and August 2024 to reverse declining business R&D intensity, the federal government executed a three-stage legislative expansion between December 2024 and November 2026.

Stage 1 — The 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) & Draft Legislation (August 15, 2025): On December 16, 2024, the federal government tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (2024 FES), proposing four foundational reforms effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024): (i) raising the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million; (ii) raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million and $50 million to $15 million and $75 million; (iii) extending the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a $15 million–$75 million three-year average gross revenue phase-out (and allowing CCPCs to elect into the revenue-based phase-out); and (iv) restoring pre-2014 eligibility rules for capital expenditures (including Shared-Use Equipment [SUE]) and equipment lease costs for property acquired or lease amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024. On August 15, 2025, the Department of Finance released formal draft legislative amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations for public consultation.

Stage 2 — Federal Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025) & Enactment of Bill C-15 (March 26, 2026): On November 4, 2025, Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne presented Budget 2025, which confirmed all measures from the 2024 FES and August 2025 draft legislation, while introducing a major enhancement: instead of increasing the annual expenditure limit to $4.5 million, Budget 2025 doubled the expenditure limit from $3.0 million to $6.0 million, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Budget 2025 projected the fiscal cost of these incremental SR&ED enhancements at $293 million over five years ($3 million in 2025–26, $70 million in 2026–27, $85 million in 2027–28, $65 million in 2028–29, and $70 million in 2029–30). On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, formally enacting the $6.0 million expenditure limit and all associated 2024 FES and Budget 2025 measures into law. Days later, on April 1, 2026, the CRA implemented its administrative modernization package, launching the elective Pre-Claim Approval regime and deploying an Enhanced AI Tool for automated claim risk assessment.

Stage 3 — Federal Budget 2026: "Masters of our Destiny" (November 5, 2026): On November 5, 2026, Minister of Finance François-Philippe Champagne tabled Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny), proposing a $930 million five-year expansion ($235 million ongoing annually thereafter) to extend SR&ED coverage "past the prototype" into commercialization and intellectual property protection. Effective for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day, November 5, 2026 (described in one practitioner summary as December 1, 2026; for calendar-year corporations, first applying to the 2027 taxation year), Budget 2026 proposes to expand eligible SR&ED activities and expenditures across three areas. First, it would include initial regulatory certification and validation studies—specifically tests, technological validations, and studies required to satisfy regulatory requirements to obtain initial approval or certification to commercialize a new or improved product or process developed through an eligible SR&ED project. Second, it would bring in intellectual property registration and maintenance costs—specifically costs incurred to register and maintain IP protection (including patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software) in Canada or under equivalent foreign law for IP developed during an eligible SR&ED project. While official filing and administrative fees paid to foreign IP offices would qualify, supporting professional activities (such as patent drafting and application preparation) would qualify only if conducted in Canada. Litigation, IP enforcement, re-certification after supplier changes, and routine surveillance audits would remain excluded, and statutory recapture rules would apply to both the SR&ED deduction and ITC if the taxpayer subsequently disposes of the protected IP. Third, Budget 2026 proposes to eliminate the requirement for certified directors' resolutions when corporations file elections or agreements to transfer qualified SR&ED expenditures (Form T1146) or allocate specified employee SR&ED wages (Form T1174), effective upon Royal Assent of the enacting legislation.
1.3 Status of the Proposed Federal Patent Box Regime

Although the Department of Finance conducted formal consultations in early 2024 on implementing a federal "patent box" (or IP box) regime to tax income derived from commercializing Canadian-developed IP at a preferential corporate tax rate—and the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and 2025 platform indicated plans to announce patent box details—neither Budget 2025 nor Budget 2026 enacted a patent box tax rate or deduction regime. Instead of introducing a back-end corporate income tax preference on IP royalty or embedded product income (which policy analysts noted would create federal-provincial revenue asymmetries unless structured as an income deduction), the federal government redirected fiscal support toward front-end commercialization and IP retention: proposing the $930 million SR&ED expansion for IP registration and regulatory certification in Budget 2026, allocating $182 million over five years in Budget 2025 for IP protection, and providing $75 million over three years (starting 2026–27) to extend the National Research Council's IP Assist Program alongside $22.5 million over three years to renew the Innovation Asset Collective's Patent Collective.

body.text: 2. Statutory & Regulatory Architecture of SR&ED Eligibility
2.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The legal foundation of every federal and provincial R&D tax claim in Canada resides in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statutory definition is structured into three core research and development categories (paragraphs (a), (b), and (c)), one derivative category of eligible support work (paragraph (d)), and seven explicit statutory exclusions (paragraphs (e) through (k)).

Under paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research), eligible work comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research typically occurs in university, institutional, or specialized industrial laboratories to discover new scientific phenomena or fundamental laws (for example, characterizing the molecular structure of a newly discovered virus). Under paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research), eligible work comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Applied research builds upon existing scientific principles to create new scientific knowledge directed toward a commercial or clinical objective (for example, investigating immunological mechanisms to formulate a vaccine against that virus). Under paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development), eligible work comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada. Crucially, the statute explicitly protects incremental improvements: a taxpayer need not invent a "new-to-the-world" product, provided the incremental improvement requires resolving genuine technological uncertainty to advance the underlying technology (such as scaling up and optimizing a bioreactor process to enable rapid, high-yield commercial vaccine manufacturing).

Under paragraph 248(1)(d) (Eligible Support Work), SR&ED also includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories—(1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support of, work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work is not SR&ED in isolation; its eligibility is strictly derivative of, and proportional ("commensurate in amount, size, extent, or duration") to, the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development it supports.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) (Statutory Exclusions / "Excluded Work") expressly exclude work with respect to: (e) market research or sales promotion (including consumer surveys, market verification, and market demonstrations); (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities (such as economics, business management, law, or classical linguistics); (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes (superficial aesthetic or cosmetic alterations that do not entail technological uncertainty); or (k) routine data collection.

As the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives emphasize, the decisive factor distinguishing eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) (such as data collection or testing) from excluded work under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k) (routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose. If testing or data collection is performed to verify commercial production quality or support normal business operations, it is excluded under paragraph (f) or (k), even if the resulting data incidentally informs R&D. Conversely, if data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of testing a hypothesis and resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty within an active SR&ED project, it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d).
2.2 Evolution of Administrative Eligibility Frameworks: From the Five Questions to the "Why" and "How" Requirements

Historically, Revenue Canada and the CRA interpreted subsection 248(1) through Information Circular IC 86-4 (issued in 1986 and revised through IC 86-4R3 in 1994), which articulated three criteria: scientific or technological uncertainty, scientific or technological advancement, and scientific and technical content. In 1998, Justice Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada decided Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520), which the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed as binding national precedent in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393). From December 2012 until August 2021, the CRA codified Justice Bowman's jurisprudence into a two-step methodology in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (revised in 2015), where Step 1 posed the canonical Five Questions:

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: On August 13, 2021 (updated July 5, 2022), following a program modernization review, the CRA archived the 2015 policy and published the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. The 2021 Guidelines reorganize the five questions into two overarching statutory requirements—The "Why" Requirement (combining Questions 1 and 4) and The "How" Requirement (combining Questions 2, 3, and 5).
1. The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty & Advancement)

Work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. To satisfy the "Why" requirement, the work must seek to generate or discover conceptual knowledge (such as explanatory theories, causal relationships, or predictive engineering models) rather than merely factual knowledge (such as raw measurements or empirical observations). Scientific or technological uncertainty arises when it is unknown or unpredictable whether a given objective or result can be achieved—or how to achieve it—due to an insufficiency in the scientific or technological knowledge base. The CRA defines the "scientific or technological knowledge base" as the combined knowledge of the resources within the claimant's business and all sources reasonably available publicly. As the Tax Court has repeatedly held (for example, JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King, 2022; Logix Data Products Inc. v. The Queen, 2022), this test is strictly objective, not subjective: a lack of internal expertise by non-engineers does not create technological uncertainty if the problem could be resolved through routine engineering or standard procedures accessible to competent professionals in the field. Consequently, acquiring existing knowledge via training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary IP does not satisfy the "Why" requirement.

The CRA Guidelines recognize seven operational characteristics indicating that standard engineering methods are insufficient and genuine technological uncertainty exists: (i) existing design methods are not applicable to the problem; (ii) required specifications or performance targets do not conform to existing industry standards; (iii) too many interdependent variables or unknowns interact simultaneously; (iv) operating parameters or environmental conditions fall outside the normal operating range; (v) the nature of the technical problem is dynamically evolving; (vi) necessary technical data is not readily available; and (vii) interlocking constraints (including system-level integration conflicts or attempting to achieve technical functionality while constrained by reasonable cost targets, as validated in Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313) prevent standard solutions from working. Whether the project ultimately succeeds or fails to achieve its technical or commercial objectives has no bearing on SR&ED eligibility; proving that a hypothesized technological approach cannot work rules out a technical avenue and advances the technological knowledge base (Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 1081).
2. The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

To satisfy the "How" requirement, the work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Trial-and-error prototyping, random parameter tweaking, or intuitive troubleshooting without structured hypothesis formulation fails technical review. A compliant systematic investigation requires four sequential steps:

items: Defining the Problem and Formulating a Hypothesis: Generating a specific technical idea, proposed method, or causal model consistent with known scientific or engineering facts that serves as a starting point for investigation aimed at resolving the identified uncertainty.

Planning and Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Designing and executing controlled physical experiments, prototype trials, mathematical analyses, or computational simulations to test the hypothesis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively based on test observations.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Analysing the empirical or analytical results to formulate logical conclusions about why the hypothesis succeeded or failed.
Maintaining Contemporaneous Evidence: Recording the hypotheses tested, experimental variables, test results, and conclusions as the work progresses.

body.text: 2.3 Grouping Work into SR&ED Projects and Determining Completion Dates

To claim SR&ED incentives on Form T661, a taxpayer must separate eligible work from ineligible commercial work and group eligible activities that relate to the same scientific or technological advancement into coherent SR&ED projects. Even if eligible experimental activities occur across multiple commercial contracts or business projects, they should be grouped into a single SR&ED project if they address the same underlying technological uncertainty and advancement.

Crucially, under CRA policy, the completion date of an SR&ED project—the point at which SR&ED eligibility ceases—occurs at the earliest of when the claimant: (i) achieves the scientific or technological advancement by resolving the associated technological uncertainties; (ii) determines that the scientific or technological uncertainties cannot be resolved; or (iii) terminates the project for any reason. For taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, under the Budget 2026 commercialization expansion, initial regulatory certification testing and IP registration costs directly linked to an eligible SR&ED project are proposed to remain claimable even after the core prototype uncertainty is resolved.
3. Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability & Pool Mechanics
3.1 Two-Tier Federal Investment Tax Credit Rate Structure
The federal SR&ED program operates a two-tier Investment Tax Credit (ITC) structure governed by subsections 127(5), 127(8), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act.

The Basic ITC Rate (15%): Set under subsection 127(9), the basic rate of 15% applies to: (i) corporations other than CCPCs and ECPCs (such as Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign multinational parents and public corporations controlled by non-residents); (ii) CCPCs and ECPCs on the portion of their annual qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds their available Expenditure Limit for the taxation year (or whose Expenditure Limit has been phased out to nil); (iii) individuals (sole proprietors) claiming on Form T2038(IND); (iv) partners of a partnership allocated ITCs under subsection 127(8); and (v) beneficiaries of trusts allocated ITCs under subsection 127(7).

The Enhanced ITC Rate (35%): Set under subsection 127(10.1), the enhanced rate of 35% (comprising the 15% basic ITC plus a 20% statutory enhancement) applies to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on their qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit.
3.2 Definition of CCPC and Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)
Corporate status is the single most consequential determinant of cash flow under the Canadian SR&ED regime, governing whether a claimant receives a 35% cash refund or a 15% non-refundable tax offset.

A Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC — Subsection 125(7)) is a private corporation and a Canadian corporation (incorporated in Canada and resident in Canada), provided it is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by a corporation with a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or by any combination thereof. Both de jure control (ownership of more than 50% of voting shares) and de facto control (subsection 256(5.1) factual influence, shareholder agreements, or convertible options and rights under paragraph 251(5)(b) granting non-residents a right to acquire shares or control) can strip a company of CCPC status (Mindready Solutions Inc., 2015 CCI 17; Aeronautic Development Corp., 2017 TCC 39; CO2 Solution Technologies Inc., 2019 CCI 286).

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 created the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC — Subsection 127(9)) category so that domestic Canadian scale-ups listing on the TSX, TSX Venture Exchange, or other designated stock exchanges no longer forfeit the 35% refundable SR&ED credit upon going public. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three statutory conditions: (1) be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year; (2) have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Furthermore, a Canadian-resident subsidiary corporation in which all or substantially all (90% or more) of the issued shares are owned by one or more ECPCs is also eligible to claim the enhanced 35% refundable ITC, sharing the consolidated group's expenditure limit.
3.3 The $6.0 Million Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas (Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue)

Under subsections 127(10.2), 127(10.21) and 127(10.6) of the Income Tax Act, as amended by Bill C-15, the maximum annual Expenditure Limit eligible for the 35% enhanced ITC rate is $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (doubled from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). Associated CCPCs must share the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and allocate it annually using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Similarly, ECPCs that are members of a corporate group preparing consolidated financial statements must share a single $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit across the consolidated group.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit phases out on a straight-line basis between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (widened from the pre-December 16, 2024 range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000) under two distinct statutory methods.
Method A: Prior-Year Taxable Capital Employed in Canada (Default for CCPCs)

By default, a CCPC's Expenditure Limit is reduced based on the taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3 of the Act / Schedule T2SCH33) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for their immediately preceding taxation year. When prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit is reduced on a straight-line basis by $0.10 for every $1.00 of taxable capital above $15,000,000, reaching nil ($0) at $75,000,000:

where:
A = max($0, min($60,000,000, Prior-Year Taxable Capital − $15,000,000))

(Note: Under the initial December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement proposal where the expenditure limit was $4,500,000 over the $60,000,000 phase-out band, the reduction factor was $0.075 per $1.00 of excess capital; under the enacted Budget 2025 / Bill C-15 $6,000,000 limit over the $60,000,000 band, the straight-line reduction rate is $6,000,000 ÷ $60,000,000 = $0.10 per $1.00 of excess capital).
Method B: Three-Year Average Annual Gross Revenue (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs)

Because public corporations do not share the same associated-CCPC taxable capital structure, an ECPC's Expenditure Limit is phased out based on its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years, as reported in the GAAP annual financial statements presented to shareholders (at the highest level of consolidation if the ECPC is part of a consolidated group, with reasonable adjustments permitted to eliminate intra-group sales of goods or services so the group reflects a single economic entity). When the three-year average annual gross revenue is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit phases out on the same straight-line trajectory ($0.10 reduction per $1.00 of average gross revenue above $15,000,000, reaching $0 at $75,000,000):
Expenditure Limit<sub>Revenue</sub> = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − R) ÷ $60,000,000
where:
R = max($0, min($60,000,000, 3-Year Average Annual Gross Revenue − $15,000,000))

Strategic Election for CCPCs: Under Bill C-15 (subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32)), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC may elect in prescribed form to calculate its Expenditure Limit using the Three-Year Average Gross Revenue method instead of the Taxable Capital method. This election is highly advantageous for capital-intensive Canadian startups and scale-ups (such as biotechnology firms in clinical trials, clean-tech developers, semiconductor companies, and hardware manufacturers) that have raised $20 million to $100 million or more in venture equity or debt (which inflates Part I.3 taxable capital above $15 million or $75 million) while remaining pre-revenue or earning less than $15 million in gross revenue. By electing the gross revenue phase-out structure, a pre-revenue CCPC with $80 million in paid-up capital—which would otherwise have a $0 Expenditure Limit under the taxable capital test—retains the full $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and up to $2,100,000 in annual cash refunds.

If a CCPC or ECPC has a taxation year of less than 51 weeks (for example, due to an incorporation, amalgamation, or acquisition of control), its calculated Expenditure Limit must be prorated under paragraph 127(10.5)(b) (paragraph 127(10.64)(b) for ECPCs) by multiplying the limit by the number of days in the short taxation year divided by 365 (or 366 if the year includes February 29).
3.4 Refundability Matrix & Qualifying Corporation Rules (Section 127.1)

Under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act (specifically subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01)), unclaimed SR&ED ITCs remaining after offsetting current-year federal Part I tax payable are refunded in cash according to the claimant's legal status, the ITC rate (35% vs. 15%), and the nature of the expenditure (current vs. capital).

For CCPCs and ECPCs earning the enhanced 35% ITC rate, unclaimed ITCs earned on current expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) are 100% refundable, providing an effective 35.0% cash refund on up to $6,000,000 of qualified current expenditures (up to $2,100,000 in cash annually). Unclaimed 35% ITCs earned on capital expenditures (for new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024) are 40% refundable, providing an effective 14.0% cash refund (40% × 35%) and a 21.0% non-refundable ITC (60% × 35%) available for carryback or carryforward.

For CCPCs earning the basic 15% ITC rate (on expenditures above their $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit), refundability depends on whether the CCPC meets the definition of a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) (and is not an "excluded corporation"). A qualifying corporation is entitled to a 40% refund on its unclaimed basic 15% ITCs, yielding an effective 6.0% cash refund (40% × 15%) and a 9.0% non-refundable ITC. Under subsection 127.1(2), a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" if its taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit is $500,000, phased out on a straight-line basis when prior-year taxable capital (associated group) is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000:

body.text: 3.5 Carryback, Carryforward, and the Subsection 37(1) Deductible Expenditure Pool

The interaction between the Section 127 ITC Pool and the Subsection 37(1) Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool is governed by strict statutory ordering and anti-double-dipping rules. Any SR&ED ITC that is refunded in cash under section 127.1 is deemed by subsection 127.1(3) to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable in the year, reducing the balance of ITCs available for carryover. Any remaining unapplied, non-refunded SR&ED ITCs may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable in those prior years (limited to current-year ITCs in excess of the amount deductible against current-year Part I tax), or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable in future years.

Instead of deducting R&D expenses under general business income rules (section 9) or depreciating capital equipment under Capital Cost Allowance (section 20(1)(a)), a taxpayer adds allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada into a running pool under subsection 37(1). The pool is increased by: current SR&ED expenditures in Canada (paragraph 37(1)(a)); capital SR&ED expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (paragraph 37(1)(b)); repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool (paragraph 37(1)(c)); prior-year negative pool balances included in income under paragraph 12(1)(v) (paragraph 37(1)(c.1)); and prior-year recaptured SR&ED ITCs (paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3)). Neither the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) nor Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) costs enter the subsection 37(1) pool.

Conversely, the subsection 37(1) pool is decreased by: government and non-government assistance—including provincial and territorial R&D tax credits—received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received (paragraph 37(1)(d)); provincial super-allowance benefits (paragraph 37(1)(d.1)); federal SR&ED ITCs claimed against tax or refunded in cash in the preceding taxation year (paragraph 37(1)(e)); amounts deducted from the pool in prior years (paragraph 37(1)(f)); insolvency deductions under section 61.3 (paragraph 37(1)(f.1)); and loss restriction event write-downs (paragraph 37(1)(h)). Under subsection 37(6.1), if a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (a loss restriction event), its subsection 37(1) pool is reduced to nil unless the same or a similar business continues to be carried on for profit.

A taxpayer may deduct all, part, or none of a positive subsection 37(1) pool balance in computing business income in a given taxation year; any undeducted positive balance carries forward indefinitely to future taxation years. (As an exception, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1), a partnership cannot carry forward a subsection 37(1) pool balance and must deduct 100% of the pool in the fiscal period incurred). Because paragraph 37(1)(e) deducts a given year's used or refunded federal SR&ED ITC from the subsection 37(1) pool in the immediately following taxation year, if the claimant deducted its full subsection 37(1) pool in Year 1 and has insufficient new SR&ED pool additions in Year 2 (or elected the Proxy Method, where the 55% PPA generates an ITC without adding to the subsection 37(1) pool), the subsection 37(1) pool will become negative at the end of Year 2. Under paragraph 12(1)(v), any negative balance in the subsection 37(1) pool at the end of a taxation year must be included in taxable business income in that year (and is then added back under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) to reset the opening pool balance for the next year to zero).
4. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs), Proxy vs. Traditional Overhead, and Restored Capital/Lease Rules
4.1 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, Foreign Wages, and the 180-Day Rule

Salaries and wages typically represent the largest component of Canadian SR&ED claims and are governed by subsections 37(8), 37(9), 37(9.1), 37(1.4), 37(1.5), 78(4), and 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations.

Under subsection 248(1), "salary or wages" means employment income computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I (sections 5 to 8 of the Act). Allowable SR&ED salaries and wages include base salary, hourly wages, regular vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, regular sick leave pay, taxable benefits under section 6 (where there is a cash outlay or reasonable cost estimate net of GST/HST/PST input tax credits), and bonuses or profit-based remuneration paid to non-specified employees. Conversely, the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy excludes four categories from direct SR&ED salary or wages. First, the employer's share of related benefits—employer contributions to CPP/QPP, Employment Insurance (EI), provincial health/payroll taxes (EHT), workers' compensation (WSIB/CNESST), pension plans, and group medical or dental insurance—is excluded from direct SR&ED wages. Under the Proxy Method, these employer benefit costs cannot be claimed separately (they are covered by the 55% PPA); under the Traditional Method, employer related benefits for hands-on SR&ED employees can be claimed as overhead on Line 360 of Form T661. Second, stock option benefits (section 7) are excluded from SR&ED expenditures for taxation years ending after November 14, 2005 (overturning Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2005 TCC 149). Third, extended vacation or sick leave (beyond normal annual entitlements) is excluded because no SR&ED duties are performed, and retiring allowances are excluded from wages (though potentially claimable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental). Fourth, shareholder dividends and non-T4 drawings are distributions of after-tax corporate profit rather than employment income under section 5, earning zero SR&ED credits.

Under the Proxy Method, only the portion of salary or wages of employees who are "directly engaged" in SR&ED in Canada (Line 300 for non-specified employees; Line 305 for specified employees) can be claimed. "Directly engaged" means hands-on technical work (performing experiments, building prototypes, writing experimental code, or direct technical supervision by first-line managers who direct the technical course of ongoing SR&ED) plus technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects. Non-specialized employees operating machinery or feeding raw materials for an experiment qualify only when directly supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications. Under the Traditional Method, in addition to hands-on staff, the incremental portion of salaries of clerical, administrative, HR, or purchasing staff who provide a direct service to hands-on SR&ED employees may be claimed as overhead on Line 360 (Regulation 2900(2)(b) and (c)).

Under subsection 248(1), a "specified employee" of a taxpayer is an employee who is a specified shareholder (owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation) OR who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, child, sibling, or controlling shareholder under section 251). Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions:

items: Prohibition on Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): No bonus or remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee may be included in SR&ED expenditures under any method.

Direct SR&ED Salary Cap of 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1)): Under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, the maximum direct SR&ED salary claimable on Line 305 of Form T661 for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the taxation year (5 × YMPE × Days ÷ 365). Associated corporations must share this 5 × YMPE limit and file Form T1174 to allocate it.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap of 75% and 2.5 × YMPE (Regulation 2900(7) and 2900(8)): When calculating the salary base for the 55% PPA in Part 5 of Form T661, the amount includable for a specified employee is restricted to the least of: (a) the actual SR&ED salary or wages claimed for the specified employee on Line 305; (b) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages from the employer in the year (including both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages); and (c) 2.5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the total number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (2.5 × YMPE × Days Employed ÷ 365), shared across associated corporations under Regulation 2900(8).

4.2 Overhead and Other Expenditures: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

To account for indirect and overhead costs associated with conducting R&D, claimants must make an irrevocable annual election for each taxation year on Part 3 of Form T661: electing the Proxy Method on Line 160 or choosing the Traditional Method on Line 162 (if neither box is ticked, the CRA processes the claim under the Traditional Method by default). Once a Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is locked and cannot be amended for that year, though the taxpayer is free to switch methods in subsequent taxation years.
1. The Proxy Method and Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(4) to 2900(10))

Under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Income Tax Act and subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, a taxpayer electing the Proxy Method does not track or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the taxpayer calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 (entered on Line 502 of Part 4) equal to 55% of the SR&ED salary base:
Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) = 55% × Eligible SR&ED Salary Base

Practitioners and claimants must ensure their working papers use the statutory 55% rate under Regulation 2900(4); the PPA rate was 65% for taxation years ending before 2013, 60% prorated for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014. The salary base comprises the SR&ED portion of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (Line 810 for non-specified employees; Line 812 for specified employees subject to the lesser of 75% of total salary and 2.5 × YMPE), excluding taxable benefits (sections 6 and 7), bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year under subsection 78(4). The PPA is a purely notional figure included in the definition of "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9) solely to earn SR&ED ITCs. It cannot be added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, actual underlying overhead expenses (such as office supplies, utilities, and clerical wages) are deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the Act.

To prevent a company whose only expenses are SR&ED salaries and building rent from claiming a notional overhead amount exceeding its actual non-SR&ED operating expenses, subsection 2900(6) caps the PPA at:
Overall PPA Cap = Total Business Deductions − Specified Deductions − Building Use/Rent Expenses

where "Specified Deductions" are amounts deducted under sections 20 (CCA and interest), 24, 26, 30, 32, 37 (the SR&ED pool deduction itself), 66 to 66.8, and 104 of the Act, and "Building Use/Rent Expenses" are outlays incurred for the use of, or right to use, a building other than a prescribed special-purpose building. In practice, as long as a business incurs at least $55 of non-rent, non-CCA general operating expenses for every $100 of SR&ED salary base, the overall cap will not bind.
2. The Traditional Method (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A), Regulation 2900(2) and 2900(3))

Under the Traditional Method, the PPA is nil (enter $0 on Line 502), and the taxpayer specifically identifies, tracks, and allocates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. Claimed Line 360 overhead enters both the subsection 37(1) deductible SR&ED pool and the qualified expenditure pool for ITCs. To qualify under Regulation 2900(2)(c) or 2900(3)(b), every overhead item must satisfy the two-part "Directly Attributable" test: (1) the Directly Related Test, requiring a direct, unmediated link connecting the expenditure to the SR&ED work, the hands-on SR&ED staff, or the machinery and equipment used to perform SR&ED; and (2) the Incremental Test, requiring that the expenditure (or claimed portion thereof) would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred (Ergorecherche et Conseils Inc. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1710; Quantetics Corporation v. The Queen, 2000 DTC 2177).
3. Cloud Computing (AWS, Azure, GCP) and Software Subscriptions: Resolving the Method Trap

A critical audit issue for modern artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), data analytics, and SaaS companies is the treatment of elastic cloud computing costs (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud GPU/CPU instances used to train experimental models) and development software licences. Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, materials must be physical, tangible substances (solid, liquid, or gas) that compose the physical body of a tangible object; cloud compute and software subscriptions are intangible services or licences and do not qualify as materials.

Under the Proxy Method, actual overhead expenses are replaced by the notional 55% PPA; consequently, cloud computing invoices and software subscriptions cannot be claimed on top of the 55% PPA (if claimed under the Proxy Method, they are disallowed on audit). Conversely, under the Traditional Method, variable cloud compute costs incurred specifically to run experimental development environments or train experimental AI/ML models (allocated separately from commercial production hosting) and incremental software tools acquired solely for SR&ED pass both the directly related and incremental tests and can be claimed on Line 360 (or, where dedicated hardware is leased after December 15, 2024, as equipment lease costs on Line 350 or Line 355). Therefore, whenever a company's provable incremental cloud compute and other directly attributable overhead exceed 55% of its SR&ED salary base, electing the Traditional Method on Line 162 yields a substantially higher SR&ED tax credit than the Proxy Method.

4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed & ITC Recapture Rules

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) and (B)(V) of the Income Tax Act, and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations, the cost of materials (including laid-down invoice cost, customs and excise duties, freight, and storage, or industrial production cost for internally manufactured inventory; excluding any non-arm's-length profit markup under subsection 127(11.6)) is claimable in the taxation year in which the materials are physically consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

The CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy defines "materials for SR&ED" as raw materials, substances, or other physical items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is being performed or that results from the SR&ED. Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers provided they are consumed or transformed in SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED (such as chemicals, reagents, growth media, seeds, or metal parts destroyed during destructive stress testing) and are not subject to ITC recapture. Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials incorporated into a prototype, pilot plant, custom commercial asset, or experimental production run (ED+EP or ED+CP) that retains residual commercial value. Where experimental development occurs alongside commercial production (ED+CP), only the incremental excess cost above standard commercial production is allowable. Furthermore, when developing a custom product or commercial asset, claimants may only claim the cost of materials transformed in the specific components involving SR&ED—not the entire commercial machine.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36), if within 20 years of acquisition a taxpayer sells or converts to commercial use any property whose cost was claimed as materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), or property acquired under an arm's-length SR&ED contract, the taxpayer triggers SR&ED ITC Recapture. The recaptured amount is added directly to federal Part I tax payable in the year of sale or conversion (and subsequently added back to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool in the following year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2)), calculated as the historical ITC rate earned on the property multiplied by the lesser of: (a) the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value at the time of conversion to commercial use); and (b) the original qualified expenditure claimed for the property. Crucially, for in-house prototypes, recapture applies only to the cost of the materials transformed—never to the in-house SR&ED salaries, wages, or overhead incurred to build the prototype (Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, Section 6.1 / 7.1).
4.4 Subcontractor Contracts vs. Third-Party Payments (80% Inclusion & Non-Arm's-Length Rules)
External R&D payments fall into two legally distinct regimes under the Income Tax Act: contracts for SR&ED performed on behalf of a claimant and third-party payments.

An SR&ED contract (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) & Subsection 127(9)) exists where a contractor performs basic research, applied research, experimental development, or support work on behalf of the claimant in Canada, where the claimant (payer) controls the work specifications and retains exclusive ownership of the resulting intellectual property. For arm's-length contracts, while 100% of the contract expenditure is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool (Line 340), subsection 127(9) restricts the amount included in "qualified expenditures" for ITC purposes to 80% of the contract cost (a 20% reduction entered on Line 529 of Form T661). Under subsection 127(9), an arm's-length contract expenditure qualifies for ITCs only if it is paid or payable to a "taxable supplier" (a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident operating through a permanent establishment in Canada subject to Part I tax) for SR&ED physically performed in Canada. Payments to foreign contractors outside Canada must be deducted in full on Line 528 of Form T661 and earn 0% ITCs. Following the restoration of capital expenditures under Bill C-15, arm's-length contract payments incurred after December 15, 2024 are no longer reduced by capital expenditures incurred by the contractor to perform the contract (former subsection 37(14)).

When a claimant subcontracts SR&ED to a non-arm's-length (NAL) party (such as a sister corporation or subsidiary), the contract payment is allowable in the payer's subsection 37(1) deductible pool (Line 345), but is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under paragraph 127(9)(f). Instead, the NAL performer claims the underlying SR&ED salaries, materials, and PPA (and the payment received is not treated as a contract payment reducing the performer's claim), or the two corporations may jointly file prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures (up to the contract price) to the payer.

By contrast, Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) & Form T1263) are payments (in cash or in kind at fair market value) made to an approved university, college, research institute, approved research association, granting council, non-profit SR&ED corporation (paragraph 149(1)(j)), or another Canadian-resident corporation where the recipient controls the R&D (typically multi-sponsor basic or applied research) and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results in its business in Canada. Third-party payments are accounted for on a cash (paid) basis, require filing prescribed Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) for each payment, enter the subsection 37(1) pool at 100% (Line 370), and enter qualified expenditures for ITC purposes at 80% (subject to the 20% reduction on Line 529). Payments used by an approved institution to acquire a building or leasehold interest in a building are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d).
4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024 Rules)

One of the most impactful provisions enacted by Bill C-15 is the restoration of SR&ED tax incentives for capital expenditures and equipment lease costs, effective for depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024, and lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024 (SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, updated June 29, 2026; SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy, updated May 22, 2026; SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, updated June 8, 2026).
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures — The ASA (≥90%) Intent Test (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) & (B)(III))

To qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure (reported on Line 390 and Box 782 of Form T661, with the 10 most expensive properties listed on Line 262), an expenditure must be incurred to acquire depreciable property (available for use under subsection 13(27) and subsection 37(1.2) after December 15, 2024) where, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended that the property would either: (1) be used during all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; OR (2) have all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Qualifying ASA capital expenditures are added in full to the subsection 37(1) pool and are 100% deductible in the year the property becomes available for use (deemed Capital Cost Allowance under subsection 37(6)); consequently, property claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance). A critical distinction applies to used depreciable property: property that has been used for any purpose prior to its acquisition by the claimant and meets the 90% ASA intent test qualifies for the 100% subsection 37(1)(b) income deduction, but is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) that is excluded from earning SR&ED Investment Tax Credits. Only new depreciable property earns the 35% (or 15%) SR&ED ITC. For CCPCs and ECPCs earning the enhanced 35% ITC rate, ITCs earned on capital expenditures are 40% refundable in cash (an effective 14% cash refund plus 21% non-refundable ITC carryforward). Non-depreciable property (land, inventory, goodwill) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (except a "special-purpose building" prescribed by the Department of Finance on a building-by-building basis under Regulation 2903) are excluded under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e). Additionally, under the Proxy Method, General-Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF—desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, photocopiers, telephones; note that computers, servers, GPUs, software, and ancillary hardware are NOT considered GPOEF and do qualify) is excluded from capital expenditures.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Subsection 127(9), Regulation 2900(11), Line 504 of Form T661)

When a taxpayer acquires new depreciable property after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA intent test (for example, a pilot manufacturing line or specialized testing instrument used 70% for SR&ED and 30% for commercial manufacturing), it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) if it is actually used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. First-Term SUE is evaluated based on actual operating time from the date the property is acquired (available for use) to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition; if SR&ED usage exceeds 50%, 25% (one-quarter) of the capital cost is included as a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes on Line 504 / Box 792 of Form T661. Second-Term SUE is evaluated from the date of acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition; if the property qualified as First-Term SUE and its cumulative actual SR&ED operating time over the 24+ month period exceeds 50%, a second 25% (one-quarter) of the capital cost is included on Line 504 (allowing up to 50% of the capital cost to earn SR&ED ITCs over two years).

Used equipment, GPOEF, and Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (property intended at acquisition to be used in the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial facility or plant, or intended to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its whole useful life) cannot qualify as SUE. Unlike ASA capital equipment, SUE capital cost does not enter the subsection 37(1) pool; it is depreciated on Schedule T2SCH8. For SUE acquired on or after September 15, 2026, under the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction (announced on September 15, 2026 and confirmed in Budget 2026), the taxpayer would be able to claim up to a 100% first-year CCA write-off on Schedule 8 on top of earning the 25% + 25% SUE SR&ED tax credit (with the ITC reducing the undepreciated capital cost [UCC] class in the following year).
3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024 — Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) & (B)(I)/(VI))

For equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024 (excluding building rent, which is barred under subparagraph 37(8)(e)(i) unless a Regulation 2903 special-purpose building): under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used ASA (≥90%) of its operating time in the tax year for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350, whereas if it is used less than 90% for SR&ED, the proportional SR&ED operating-time percentage is claimable as overhead on Line 360 provided the lease is directly related and incremental to SR&ED. Under the Proxy Method, GPOEF and land leases are excluded; if eligible leased equipment is used ASA (≥90%) for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350, if used primarily (>50% and <90%) for SR&ED, 50% (half) of the lease cost is claimed on Line 355, and if used 50% or less, 0% is claimable.
4.6 Unpaid Current Expenditures (Subsection 127(26)) and Prescribed Excluded Expenditures (Regulation 2902)

Under subsection 127(26) of the Income Tax Act, any current SR&ED expenditure (other than salary or wages governed by subsection 78(4)) that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred stays in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool for that year, but must be deducted from qualified expenditures on Line 520 of Form T661 so that it does not earn an ITC until the taxation year in which it is actually paid. If an unpaid expenditure is not explicitly identified on Form T661 within the 18-month reporting deadline for the year it was incurred, it will never qualify to earn an ITC even when subsequently paid. Furthermore, if the unpaid item is an arm's-length SR&ED contract, 20% is deducted on Line 529 and the remaining 80% is deducted as unpaid on Line 520; when paid in a later year, only 80% of the payment is added to qualified expenditures.

Finally, section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations (reported on Line 530 of Form T661) designates specific prescribed expenditures that cannot be included in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes, even if directly related and incremental to SR&ED:

items: Legal or accounting fees—including all consulting and professional fees paid to prepare, file, or defend an SR&ED claim (Regulation 2902(a)(i)(B));
Interest and financing costs described in paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g) of the Act (Regulation 2902(a)(i)(C));
Entertainment expenses, advertising or selling expenses, and convention or conference expenses (Regulation 2902(a)(i)(D)–(F));
Dues or membership fees in a scientific or technical society or organization, and fines or penalties (Regulation 2902(a)(i)(G)–(H)); and
Expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (subsection 37(4) and Regulation 2902(c)).

body.text: 5. Provincial & Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes (All 13 Jurisdictions)

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits that stack on top of the federal SR&ED program, while three jurisdictions (Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut) offer no provincial or territorial credit. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, every provincial or territorial R&D tax credit is legally classified as "government assistance" that reduces the federal subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base (unless the taxpayer formally waives or renounces the provincial credit on or before its filing-due date).
5.1 Québec — Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

In its 2025–2026 Budget (Information Bulletin 2025-6), the Government of Québec enacted a comprehensive structural overhaul of provincial innovation taxation. Effective for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec repealed seven legacy R&D tax incentives and consolidated its innovation support into a single flagship measure administered by Revenu Québec: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation).

The seven abolished Québec tax measures (repealed for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, though still claimable for taxation years that began before March 26, 2025) are: (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly Form RD-1029.7-V, which provided a 14% basic rate and up to 30% for SMEs based on global assets); (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (formerly Form RD-1029.8.6-V); (3) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (formerly Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V); (4) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (formerly Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V); (5) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; (6) the industrial design component of the Design Tax Credit (the fashion design component remains in force); and (7) the five-year Personal Income Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts.

The CRIC is 100% refundable for all eligible corporations operating a business in Québec with an establishment in Québec (not restricted to CCPCs—foreign-controlled subsidiaries and large public corporations also qualify for the 30% rate on the first $1.0 million). A 30% enhanced refundable rate applies to the first $1,000,000 of qualified CRIC expenditures that exceed the corporation's Applicable Exclusion Threshold (regardless of the corporation's asset size; associated corporations operating in Québec must share the $1,000,000 limit via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and a 20% basic refundable rate applies to all qualified CRIC expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 threshold, with no upper expenditure ceiling (and 20% applies to a corporate partner's share of partnership CRIC expenditures above the partnership's exclusion threshold).

The CRIC covers two distinct pillars of work carried out in Québec: (1) Scientific Research and Experimental Development (R&D), which is harmonized with the federal definition under subsection 248(1) of the ITA (basic research, applied research, and experimental development), with the CRA conducting the scientific review of the R&D component; and (2) Eligible Pre-Commercialization Activities, comprising activities carried out in Québec in conjunction with (and in continuation of) R&D work performed in Québec by or on behalf of the claimant—specifically (a) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements and aimed at obtaining an initial registration, approval, or certification to commercialize an innovation (including implementing a quality control system required for initial certification), and (b) product design, including developing form and aesthetics, improving functionality, and selecting materials.

Unlike the federal program, Québec does not use a 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount and does not include raw materials in the CRIC base. Qualified CRIC expenditures incurred in Québec consist of four categories (less government and non-government assistance): (1) 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities performed in Québec; (2) 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors (arm's-length) for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization contracts carried out in Québec; (3) 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity; and (4) 100% of capital property acquisition costs to acquire new depreciable property (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings, and excluding property used in a certified Large Investment Project tax holiday) used in Québec for R&D or pre-commercialization. If capital property ceases to be used solely in Québec for R&D or pre-commercialization within a minimum period of 730 consecutive days following the start of its use, Revenu Québec recovers the CRIC via a special recapture tax.
Before applying the 30% and 20% CRIC rates, total qualified expenditures must be reduced by the corporation's Exclusion Threshold for the taxation year, which equals the greater of:
Exclusion Threshold<sub>CRIC</sub> = max($50,000, Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> (Basic Personal Amount × %Time<sub>i, R&D + Pre-Comm</sub>))

where the Basic Personal Amount of the Québec personal income tax system is multiplied by the proportion of time each employee i devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities during the year (the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold). The CRIC is claimed by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (accompanied by Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization activities, Form RD-1029.8.EN-T for associated group limit allocation, and Form RD-222-V for the Québec R&D deduction pool) with the Québec CO-17 corporate income tax return within 18 months of fiscal year-end. The same expenditure cannot be claimed for both the CRIC and another Québec tax credit (such as the C3i Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation).
5.2 Ontario — OITC (8%), ORDTC (3.5%), and OBRITC (20%)

Ontario operates three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA through the federal T2 return and contingent on timely filing of federal Form T661 within 18 months of year-end.

First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007; Schedule 566) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures per year (maximum annual cash credit of $240,000, shared across associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years). Ontario has not increased the OITC cap from $3.0 million to $6.0 million. Unlike the federal enhanced credit, the OITC $3,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by both prior-year taxable income and prior-year specified capital (on an associated group basis): it phases out on a straight-line basis when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, OR when prior-year Ontario specified paid-up or taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Per Ontario's Fall Economic Statement annex, 100% of qualified capital expenditures on depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 are eligible for the OITC (and ORDTC). The OITC is claimed on Schedule 566 (Schedule 5 Line 468) and may be waived in whole or in part under subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38–45 of the Taxation Act, 2007; Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment (including large corporations, public companies, and foreign-controlled subsidiaries), with no expenditure cap, no taxable income test, and no taxable capital phase-out. Because the OITC (and OBRITC) is treated as government assistance under Ontario law, a corporation claiming both OITC and ORDTC must first subtract its current-year OITC entitlement from its gross Ontario eligible expenditures before multiplying by 3.5% (ORDTC = 3.5% × [Gross Ontario Eligible Spend − OITC − OBRITC]). Unused ORDTC carries back 3 years and forward 20 years. Recapture applies if claimed SR&ED property is sold or converted to commercial use under section 45 (calculated using the statutory 23.56% rate and reported on Schedule 5 Line 277). The ORDTC is claimed on Schedule 508 (Schedule 5 Line 416) and may be waived under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario).

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007; Schedules 568 & 569) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures paid under an eligible contract with an approved Ontario research institute (university, college, or hospital research institute), up to a maximum annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (maximum $4,000,000 refundable credit, shared among associated corporations), claimed on Schedule 568 and Schedule 569 (Schedule 5 Line 470).
5.3 British Columbia — B.C. SR&ED Tax Credit (Full Bill C-15 Alignment & Permanent Status)

Governed by Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and amended by Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), British Columbia's SR&ED tax credit is administered by the CRA and is the provincial program that expressly aligned with all principal federal Bill C-15 reforms. B.C. Budget 2026 repealed the former September 1, 2027 sunset clause, making the B.C. SR&ED tax credit permanent.

Effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, both qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a B.C. permanent establishment earn a 10% fully refundable tax credit on up to the $6,000,000 federal Expenditure Limit (doubling the maximum B.C. cash refund from $300,000 to $600,000 per year), phased out over the expanded $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital (or three-year average gross revenue) range. Expenditures above the $6,000,000 limit and expenditures incurred by non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporations earn a 10% non-refundable credit, which carries back 3 years and forward 10 years. Capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 are restored to the B.C. qualified expenditure base. The credit is claimed on Form T666 (British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit, also designated as Schedule 425 in T2 software; Schedule 5 Line 674 for refundable and Line 659 for non-refundable) within 18 months of the end of the taxation year.
5.4 Alberta — Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Governed by Division 7 of Part 6 (sections 26.95 to 26.99) of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and administered independently by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (Tax and Revenue Administration [TRA]), the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a two-tier incremental refundable tax credit on eligible R&D carried out in Alberta. Under Tier 1 (8% Base Refundable Rate), every dollar of current-year eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's Base Amount (or maximum expenditure limit, if lower) earns an 8% refundable grant, where the Base Amount is the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years (Base Amount = [SpendT−2 + SpendT−1] ÷ 2). Under Tier 2 (20% Incremental Refundable Rate), every dollar of current-year eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the two-year average Base Amount earns an additional 12% incremental payment on top of the 8% base rate, yielding a combined 20% refundable grant on the incremental slice. A first-time R&D claimant in Alberta with $0 spending in the prior two years has a Base Amount of $0 and earns the full 20% refundable rate on 100% of its eligible spend up to $4.0 million.

Annual eligible expenditures are capped at $4,000,000 (prorated for short years and shared among associated corporations), for a maximum possible annual cash grant of $800,000 ($4,000,000 × 20%). The $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit phases out on a straight-line basis when prior-year federal taxable capital employed in Canada (Line 690 of Schedule T2SCH33) is between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000:
Maximum Expenditure Limit<sub>IEG</sub> = $4,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − (Taxable Capital − $10,000,000)) ÷ $40,000,000

and is eliminated at $50,000,000. Any corporation (not only CCPCs) below the $50 million taxable capital ceiling is eligible for the refundable IEG. Alberta did not adopt the federal $6.0 million cap or $15M–$75M phase-out, and per updated Alberta TRA instructions on AT1 Schedule 29, for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, claimants must pull their starting federal expenditure figure from Line 557 of Form T661 (current SR&ED expenditures only) rather than Line 559—thereby excluding restored federal capital expenditures from the Alberta IEG calculation. The grant is claimed by filing AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Claimed in Alberta) with the Alberta AT1 corporate tax return within 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date (21 months after year-end), contingent on filing federal Form T661 with the CRA within 18 months of year-end.
5.5 Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, Yukon, and Non-Credit Jurisdictions

In Saskatchewan (Section 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan); Schedule 403), the CRA administers a 10% R&D tax credit. For qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, Saskatchewan doubled the 10% refundable threshold for CCPCs from the first $1,000,000 to the first $2,000,000 of eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures (maximum $200,000 annual cash refund) and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures. Expenditures by CCPCs above $2,000,000 and all expenditures by non-CCPCs (including ECPCs) earn a 10% non-refundable credit (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years, with a waiver option under subsection 63.4(13)), and total combined refundable and non-refundable credits are subject to an annual cap of $1,000,000 per corporation/group ($10,000,000 of spend).

In Manitoba (Section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba); Schedule 380), the CRA administers a 15% tax credit on eligible Manitoba SR&ED expenditures (including both current expenditures and depreciable capital property other than buildings, as Manitoba never repealed capital eligibility), with no expenditure cap. For in-house R&D, 50% of the credit is refundable (an effective 7.5% cash refund) and 50% is non-refundable (an effective 7.5% non-refundable credit that carries back 3 years and forward 20 years). When R&D is performed under an eligible contract with a qualifying Manitoba post-secondary educational or research institution, 100% of the 15% credit is refundable in cash.

In the Atlantic Provinces and Yukon, four jurisdictions provide flat 15% fully refundable tax credits administered by the CRA with no expenditure cap and no CCPC restriction: Nova Scotia (Section 41 of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia); Schedule 340; recapture applies; can be renounced within 6 months of year-end); New Brunswick (New Brunswick Income Tax Act; Schedule 360; recapture applies); Newfoundland and Labrador (Section 42 of the Income Tax Act, 2000 (NL); Schedule 301 / Form T1129; available to corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnerships, with the unique statutory rule that eligible expenditures are not reduced by other government or non-government assistance except GST/HST input tax credits); and Yukon (Income Tax Act (Yukon); Schedule 442 / Form T1232; 15% refundable credit plus an additional 5% refundable bonus credit [20% total] on eligible amounts paid or payable to Yukon University). Finally, Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit; claimants in these three jurisdictions claim the federal SR&ED credit (35% or 15%) unreduced by any provincial R&D tax credit assistance.
